text: in Idaho To help decide the appropriate switchover temperatures, we looked at the distribution of the average heating and cooling loads during the peak period across various daily average temperatures, as shown in Figure 11 and Figure 12. 2 Preheating does not require raising the cooling set point by default—it only requires raising the heating set point; however, to prevent an inverted set point (where the cooling set point is lower than the heating set point), the algorithm raises the cooling set point as well when the heating set point exceeds the cooling set point. 21 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 11. State average hourly cooling load per building during the peak period Figure 12. State average hourly heating load per building during the peak period The average load at a given average daily temperature for a given state varies among different days (different dots in the figure), depending on the specific temperature profile for the day and the internal heat generated in the building via various occupancy-driven end uses. Figure 11 shows minimal cooling below an average daily temperature of 10°C (50°F), and Figure 12 shows minimal heating above an average daily temperature of 25°C (68°F). Based on these results, in the final implementation, we precooled only if the daily average temperature is above 68°F, and we preheated only if the daily average temperature is below 50°F. We did not need to follow these thresholds for load shedding—decreasing the heating set point and increasing the cooling set point during the peak period will reduce the demand regardless of the building having a cooling or a heating load. 22 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4.3 Final Sensitivity Analysis After further reviewing the real-world demand response programs and reviewing the initial sensitivity analysis results, we narrowed the analysis space. First, we narrowed the offset to only 2–4°F, and then we limited the precooling windows to 1 hour and 4 hours. More details can be seen in Table 7. In this round, we also introduced a random shift. This was used to reduce the “snapback,” or rebound, seen after the peak period when all thermostats reset to the normal set point at the same time. A maximum random shift of ± 30 minutes will make some buildings start their peak period up to 30 minutes early or up to 30 minutes late (i.e., the shift can be anything ranging from +30 minutes, to +15 minutes, to 0 minutes, to -15 minutes, to -30 minutes). This random shifting was assigned on a building-by-building basis, not on a per-event basis. In a real deployment, this staggering of individual homes could be accomplished through a combination of intentional control, inherent time delays, and equipment states found across the portfolio at any point in time. 23 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
